nameStory: This fungus gets its scientific name from the Latin 'annulus' meaning ring, referring to the distinctive flat, disk-like rings that circle the tiny openings on its surface. While it doesn't have a widely-used common name, some mycologists call it the 'ringed carbon cushion' for these telltale rings and its black, cushion-like appearance.
description: This is a hard, black fungus that forms cushion-shaped or semi-round bumps on dead hardwood trees, especially oak. The surface is covered with tiny pimple-like bumps, each surrounded by a distinctive flat ring that you might need a magnifying glass to see clearly. These tough, carbonaceous fungi are part of nature's cleanup crew, slowly decomposing dead wood. Individual fruiting bodies can range from small bumps to cushions several inches across.

idTips.label: Ringed openings
idTips.description: Tiny pimple-like bumps on the surface are each surrounded by a flat, disk-like ring - use a hand lens to see this distinctive feature clearly

idTips.label: Black cushion shape
idTips.description: Hard, coal-black fruiting bodies that feel like charcoal and form semi-round, cushion-like bumps protruding from the wood

idTips.label: Oak preference
idTips.description: Almost always found growing on dead oak wood - logs, branches, or stumps of various oak species

idTips.label: Chemical test
idTips.description: When crushed and mixed with household lye or potassium hydroxide, produces a distinctive olive-green color

idTips.label: Hard texture
idTips.description: Feels like a piece of charcoal or hard carbon - very firm and brittle, not spongy like many other fungi

habitat: Look for this fungus on dead oak trees throughout New England's forests, from coastal areas to mountainous regions. It thrives on fallen logs, dead branches, and oak stumps in both mixed hardwood forests and oak-dominated woodlands. You'll find it wherever oaks grow, from sea level up into the mountains.

seasonality.spring: Existing fruiting bodies from previous years remain visible and identifiable, though new growth may just be beginning to emerge from the wood.
seasonality.summer: Active growing season when new black cushions develop and mature, making this an excellent time for identification and study.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for spotting mature fruiting bodies, which stand out prominently against fallen autumn leaves and are releasing spores.
seasonality.winter: Hard, persistent fruiting bodies remain clearly visible on bare wood and are often easier to spot without leaf cover obscuring the view.

funFact: This fungus is essentially a biological cannon - it builds up pressure inside its tiny flask-shaped chambers and literally shoots its spores out through those ringed openings, sometimes launching them several inches away to find new dead wood to colonize!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other black, crusty fungi on dead wood, but the distinctive flat rings around each tiny opening are unique - think of them as tiny bull's-eyes that no other local species has.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name changed relatively recently in 2005 when mycologists split these ringed species off from the larger Hypoxylon genus, so you might find older field guides listing this under its former name Hypoxylon annulatum.
compareHints: Unlike its relative Cramp Balls (which forms smooth, ball-like masses), this species has the distinctive flat rings around its openings and grows in more cushion-like shapes. Cramp Balls also tend to be more spherical and lack the organized ring pattern that makes this species so distinctive.
